facts: The writ petitioner has by the present application under Article 32 of the Constitution challenged the order of his detention dated 7.11.1987, passed under Section 3(2) of the National Security Act, 1980.
Earlier he had unsuccessfully moved the Allahabad High Court under Article 226.
The District Magistrate has mentioned three incidents in the grounds served on the petitioner:
The writ petitioner was in custody and moved an application for bail.

Criminal cases were registered against the petitioner with respect to each of the three incidents but it appears that evidence against the petitioner was not forthcoming, although several persons supported the prosecution version of the third incident dated 27.7.1987 by their statements recorded under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
issues: Whether the order of detention is vitiated on several counts.
Whether the delay in passing the detention order is sufficient to strike it down.
Whether the District Magistrate had jurisdiction to detain the petitioner with a view to frustrate the Criminal Court's order enlarging the petitioner on bail.
petitioner_arguments: The order of detention is vitiated on several counts.
As only one of the three incidents mentioned in the grounds can be held to be connected with the public order problem, the order must be held to be bad.
It was wrong for the District Magistrate and the High Court to have referred to the first two incidents.
The order having been passed on account of the third incident which happened more than four months earlier ought to be set aside on the ground of undue delay alone.

The order was vitiated as the petitioner's bail application in the Criminal Court was not opposed by the State; and in any view the District Magistrate had no jurisdiction for detaining the petitioner with a view to frustrate the Criminal Court's order enlarging the petitioner on bail.
respondent_arguments: The detention order was passed with a view to prevent the petitioner from indulging in activities prejudicial to the maintenance of public order.
The District Magistrate came to this conclusion on the consideration of relevant materials.
Copies of the documents were served on the petitioner along with the grounds.
court_reasoning: It is necessary to consider the circumstances in each individual case to find out whether the delay has been satisfactorily explained or not.

The distinction between such delay and the delay in complying with the procedural safeguards of Article 22(5) of the Constitution as pointed out in Rajendra kumar Natvarlal Shah v. State of Gujarat & Ors., [1988] 3 SCC 153 1988 Indlaw SC 71.
The District Magistrate was expecting an adverse order on account of the fact that the witnesses of the incident appeared to be reluctant to support their earlier statements.
holding: We do not find any merit in the plea that the impugned order is bad on account of delay.
We also do not find any force in this argument as it cannot be presumed that the petitioner was prejudiced by non-service of a copy of his own application.
There is no merit whatsoever in the petitioner's grievance of discrimination on the ground that the other co-accused persons have not been detained.
